lead: No natural product has been shown in repeated large trials to slow Alzheimer's disease or to prevent dementia; one trial found high-dose vitamin E slowed loss of daily function. In people who already have Alzheimer's, omega-3 (DHA) and high-dose B vitamins did not slow decline in placebo-controlled trials (grade: Negative). Vitamin E, vitamin D, ginkgo and multivitamins each have a positive trial or mixed results, mostly on test scores rather than dementia itself (grade B).

grade_key.A: Meta-analysis, or at least 2 randomized trials with low risk of bias and a consistent benefit
grade_key.B: 1 good randomized trial, or several randomized trials with mixed results
grade_key.C: Observational studies, small pilots or open-label trials only
grade_key.Negative: Randomized trials found no benefit over placebo

disclaimer: This page summarizes published research. It is not medical advice. Talk to a clinician before starting any supplement, especially if you take other medicines.

products.name: Ginkgo biloba
products.summary: Treatment: a 2026 Cochrane review compared ginkgo with placebo. In 13 studies with 3,288 people with dementia, it found low-certainty evidence of small to moderate benefits at six months on global status, cognition and daily activities. In 12 studies of mild cognitive impairment, ginkgo probably had little or no effect. Prevention: two large placebo-controlled trials found no reduction in dementia. In one, 3,069 people aged 75 or older took 120 mg twice a day or placebo and were followed for a median of 6.1 years; the other followed 2,854 older adults for 5 years and found no reduction in progression to Alzheimer's disease.
products.safety_interactions: The Cochrane review found probably little or no difference in adverse events between ginkgo and placebo in dementia. In the two prevention trials adverse effects were similar with ginkgo and placebo, and in the 5-year trial strokes and other bleeding events did not differ. A review of 15 published case reports found a possible causal link between ginkgo and bleeding, including 8 bleeds inside the skull, although most cases had other bleeding risks. A hospital records study found that ginkgo prescribed with medicines including clopidogrel and aspirin was associated with bleeding and abnormal clotting tests.

general_safety.name: Ginkgo biloba
general_safety.short: Trials of clotting measures indicate no higher bleeding risk, but case reports describe bleeding, including intracranial. Interactions with anticoagulant or antiplatelet medicines cannot be ruled out.

products.name: Multivitamin-mineral supplements
products.summary: Prevention: in COSMOS-Mind, a 3-year trial in 2,262 older adults, a daily multivitamin-mineral led to slightly better global cognition scores than placebo, and a meta-analysis of three COSMOS substudies estimated the effect as equal to about 2 years less cognitive ageing. The same trial found no reduction in new cases of mild cognitive impairment or dementia, though it had low statistical power for this. In the Physicians' Health Study II, 5,947 male physicians aged 65 or older who took a daily multivitamin had no cognitive benefit. Treatment: no randomized trials of general multivitamins in people with Alzheimer's disease were found in a PubMed search on 23 November 2026; a trial of a B-vitamin-based supplement is described under B vitamins.
products.safety_interactions: No safety data found in the cited trials.

general_safety.name: Multivitamin and mineral supplements
general_safety.short: COSMOS found no safety concerns or change in all-cause mortality with a daily multivitamin; Physicians' Health Study II found no change in cancer deaths.

products.name: Vitamin D
products.summary: Treatment: a 12-month trial in 210 people with Alzheimer's disease compared 800 IU of vitamin D a day with placebo and reported a larger increase in full-scale IQ and better scores on several cognitive subtests, with lower amyloid-related blood markers; the authors called for larger, longer trials. Prevention: in two substudies of the VITAL trial in older adults, 2,000 IU of vitamin D3 a day did not change the rate of cognitive decline over 2 to 3 years. A Cochrane review found no effect of 400 IU of vitamin D3 with calcium on dementia incidence. In a cohort of 12,388 people without dementia, taking vitamin D was associated with 40% lower dementia incidence; a cohort study cannot show that vitamin D caused this.
products.safety_interactions: No safety data found in the cited trials.

general_safety.name: Vitamin D
general_safety.short: Long-term supplementation raised the risk of high blood calcium and high urine calcium in trials, but not kidney stones; toxicity from extremely high doses is rare but serious.

products.name: Vitamin E (alpha-tocopherol)
products.summary: Treatment: in a trial of 561 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease followed for about 2.3 years, 2,000 IU a day of alpha-tocopherol slowed decline in daily activities compared with placebo, a delay of about 6 months over the follow-up. A Cochrane review found no evidence that vitamin E improves cognition in Alzheimer's disease or mild cognitive impairment, or that it prevents progression from mild cognitive impairment to dementia. Prevention: a Cochrane review of vitamin and mineral trials in cognitively healthy people found low-certainty evidence of no effect of vitamin E on dementia incidence.
products.safety_interactions: The Cochrane review in Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment found no increase in serious adverse events or deaths with vitamin E. In a cancer-prevention trial in healthy men, included in the other Cochrane review, prostate cancer diagnoses increased among men taking vitamin E. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Vitamin E
general_safety.short: Meta-analyses link vitamin E to more haemorrhagic strokes and, at high doses, higher mortality; in the SELECT trial it raised prostate cancer risk in healthy men.

products.name: B vitamins (folic acid, B6, B12)
products.summary: Treatment: an 18-month trial in 409 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease tested high-dose folic acid, vitamin B6 and vitamin B12 against placebo and found no slowing of cognitive decline. A 26-week trial in 89 people with Alzheimer's taking a cholinesterase inhibitor found no difference in cognition or daily function. A 2024 meta-analysis of 5 trials in Alzheimer's found slightly better MMSE scores with B12 and folic acid but no difference on the ADAS-Cog or in daily life function. In mild cognitive impairment, a Cochrane review of 5 trials found no evidence of benefit on cognition; one 2-year trial found slower brain shrinkage on MRI. Prevention: a Cochrane review of 14 trials in 27,882 cognitively healthy adults found B vitamins probably have little or no effect on overall cognition. A Japanese cohort study linked higher dietary riboflavin (vitamin B2), measured from a single 24-hour food recall, to a lower risk of disabling dementia; this is an association from diet, not a supplement trial.
products.safety_interactions: In the 18-month Alzheimer's trial, more depression-related adverse events occurred with the vitamins than with placebo. The 2-year trial in mild cognitive impairment found no difference in serious adverse events. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited trials.

general_safety.name: B vitamins
general_safety.short: High vitamin B6 levels, usually from supplements, may cause sensory nerve damage. Folic acid did not change cancer rates over about 5 years in large trials.

products.name: Omega-3 fatty acids (DHA and EPA)
products.summary: Treatment: a Cochrane review of 3 placebo-controlled trials in 632 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease found no convincing benefit of omega-3 supplements, and rated the evidence high quality. The largest, an 18-month trial of 2 g a day of algal DHA in 402 people, did not slow cognitive or functional decline. A 2024 meta-analysis of 14 studies, which also pooled a combined nutrient product, reported slower progression on the Clinical Dementia Rating scale but no difference on the MMSE, ADAS-cog or daily-activity scales. Prevention: a Cochrane review of trials in cognitively healthy older people found no benefit on cognition, and a 3-year trial in 1,680 older people with memory complaints found no effect on cognitive decline. In the Framingham cohort of 1,490 people without dementia, those with the highest red-blood-cell DHA had a 49% lower risk of Alzheimer's than those with the lowest; this is an association and does not show that DHA caused the difference.
products.safety_interactions: In the Cochrane treatment review, two trials reported that all adverse events were mild and no more frequent than with placebo. The prevention review found mild gastrointestinal problems were the main side effect, and the 3-year prevention trial raised no safety concerns. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Omega-3 fatty acids
general_safety.short: Linked to a higher risk of atrial fibrillation in cardiovascular trials, more so above 1 g/day; diarrhoea and altered taste were more likely than with placebo; bleeding findings are mixed.

products.name: Turmeric and curcumin
products.summary: Treatment: in a 24-week placebo-controlled trial, 36 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease took 2 or 4 grams of curcumin a day or placebo; there were no differences in clinical or biomarker measures, and blood levels of curcumin were low. A 2019 meta-analysis found that, in the Alzheimer's trials it pooled, people taking curcumin tended to do worse than those on placebo on the MMSE. The trials are small, so this Negative grade rests on limited evidence. Prevention: trials in healthy older adults measure test scores, not dementia, and are not summarised here; claims that curcumin protects against Alzheimer's rest mainly on laboratory and animal work.
products.safety_interactions: In the 24-week trial, 3 people taking curcumin withdrew because of gastrointestinal symptoms, and curcumin was linked to lower haematocrit and higher glucose that the authors judged clinically insignificant. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Turmeric and curcumin
general_safety.short: Case series link turmeric supplements to liver injury, sometimes severe. Curcumin may alter levels of some drugs, including anticoagulants, mostly in non-clinical studies.
